Ch 4 · Solution concepts for games

What counts as a solution?

Edit any payoff, or load a classic game. The page finds best responses, pure and mixed Nash equilibria, Pareto-optimal outcomes, the welfare and fairness optima, and each agent's maxmin (security) value.

Blue = agent 1's reward, orange = agent 2's reward. An underlined reward is a best response to the other agent's action. Tags: NE pure Nash, PO Pareto-optimal, W max welfare (sum), F max fairness (product).

Equilibria

Correlated equilibria by linear programming

§4.6 · LP Eq. 4.20–4.23

A correlated equilibrium is a joint distribution over joint actions. A mediator samples a joint action and privately tells each agent its own part. It is an equilibrium if no agent gains by deviating from its recommendation (CE), or by committing in advance to any fixed action instead (coarse CE). The book finds one by linear programming over the probabilities x_a. Change the game or the objective and the LP re-solves.

Incentive check: follow or deviate?

For each recommendation, the expected reward of following it (under the conditional distribution of the other agent’s recommendation) is compared with the best deviation. All rows must be green for a CE. For a coarse CE the comparison is made before the recommendation is seen.

Four problems a single-agent learner never meets

Non-stationarity

§5.4.1

In the Stag Hunt, agent 1's value for each action depends on π₂. When agent 2 learns, the target agent 1 is chasing moves.

0.80

Equilibrium selection

§5.4.2Our simulation

Two agents run gradient ascent from every starting policy. The color shows which equilibrium each start ends in. Click the map to trace a single run.

Multi-agent credit assignment

§5.4.3

Three agents share one reward: +1 if the levels of the agents who try to collect a level-3 item add up to at least 3. Toggle who collects. A difference reward asks what would change if only this agent had done nothing.

Scaling to many agents

§5.4.4

The joint action space grows as |A|ⁿ. A central learner needs one value per joint action; independent learners need n·|A|.

Bar lengths use a log scale (powers of 10).

From challenge to remedy

Ch 5.3.3 · Central vs independent Q-learning

Train two foragers from scratch

This is the book's Figure 5.3 task, shrunk to fit a browser. Two level-1 agents start in the top corners. The level-1 item can be collected by one agent; the level-2 item needs both agents to load at the same time. Central Q-learning (CQL) explores 36 joint actions per state; independent Q-learning (IQL) explores 6 per agent.

Central vs independent Q-learning

§5.3.3 · Fig. 5.3
Differs from the bookThe book’s task uses an 11 × 11 grid. This runs on a 5 × 5 or 7 × 7 grid so it trains in seconds.

Each point is the discounted return (γ = 0.99, both agents' rewards summed) of one greedy evaluation episode. ε decays linearly from 1 to 0.05 and α = 0.05. Start a new run with the other algorithm to overlay both curves. The maximum return is below 1 because of discounting.

Ch 9.3–9.5 · Independent learning, multi-agent policy gradient, value decomposition

Critics, mixers and what they condition on

Six architectures from Chapter 9. Solid arrows are used at execution; dashed arrows exist only during centralized training.

Value decomposition lab

§9.5.4Trained live

Both methods are fitted to a common-reward matrix game with uniform data, like the book's experiments. VDN is solved in closed form (least-squares sum of two utilities). QMIX trains a small monotonic mixing network in your browser with Adam. The greedy joint action picks each agent's highest utility, with no communication between them.

QMIX in detail: agent networks, hypernetworks, mixing network

§9.5.3 · Alg. 22

Counterfactual baseline calculator

§9.4.4 · Eq. 9.15–9.16

Fix the other agents’ actions a₋ᵢ. The critic gives Q for each of agent i’s own actions. Set agent i’s policy and the action it actually took, and compare three ways to weight the policy gradient.

Two-step game: why value accuracy matters

Figures 9.13–9.14

In the first step there is no reward, and agent 1 alone picks the next game: A leads to the linear game and B to the monotonic game. The optimal plan is B, then (B, B) for 10. Each method is trained here on all joint actions (γ = 1) with tabular utilities, a small per-state mixing network for QMIX, and QTRAN-base losses.

Ch 9.6–9.7 · Agent modeling · homogeneous agents

Sharing parameters, sharing experience, modeling others

Three ways to exploit what agents have in common, or to reason about how they differ.

Experience sharing, live

§9.7.2 · Alg. 24Tabular analog

Two runs on the 7×7 foraging task. In both, each agent keeps its own Q-table over an egocentric state (its own position first) and learns by sampling transitions from a replay buffer. In one run each agent samples only its own experience; in the other both agents sample from a shared buffer. Level-based foraging agents are weakly homogeneous, so each agent can learn from the other’s experience. This is a tabular stand-in for DQN with a shared replay buffer.

Ch 9.8–9.9 · Policy self-play · population-based training

Getting stronger by playing yourself

AlphaZero learns one policy by playing against itself. PSRO keeps a population of policies and repeatedly best-responds to a mixture of them. AlphaStar's league training follows a similar approach to PSRO, with specialized agent roles.

AlphaZero training loop

AlphaStar league

MCTS, one phase at a time

§9.8.1 · Alg. 25

A tiny decision problem: three binary choices lead to one of eight terminal rewards (shown along the bottom, hidden from the search). Each simulation runs four phases: select actions with UCB inside the tree, expand one new node, evaluate it with a random rollout, and back-propagate the return u. Edge labels show N (visits) and Q (average return).

The PSRO loop

PSRO step by step

§9.9.1

Meta-game Mk

Meta-solver: Nash δk

Best-response gain (exploitability)

Symmetric zero-sum game, so one population serves both agents. The oracle returns an exact best response to δk. The chart shows how much the oracle’s best response gains against δk in the full game, often called exploitability (a common term the book does not use). It reaches 0 exactly when δk is a Nash equilibrium of the full game, which is the book’s convergence result in §9.9.2.

Prioritized fictitious self-play weighting

Eq. 9.98

AlphaStar picks opponents with probability ∝ f(P[win]). fhard(x) = (1 − x)p focuses on opponents the learner still loses to. fvar(x) = x(1 − x) focuses on opponents of similar strength.

      Check yourself

      What changed?

      Each question names two methods of the lineage; pick the one change between them.

      1What does QMIX change about VDN?

      §9.5.3: QMIX aggregates the agents’ utilities with a mixing network whose weights come from a hypernetwork and stay positive, so the mix is monotonic; VDN uses a sum.

      2What does independent Q-learning change about Q-learning?

      Alg. 5 (§5.3.2): each agent i learns Qᵢ over its own actions aᵢ and reward rᵢ, and treats the other agents as part of the environment.

      3What does a centralized critic change about independent A2C?

      §9.4.2: only the critic changes. The actor π(aᵢ | hᵢ) still uses the agent’s own history, so execution stays decentralized.

      Race

      Every method the Lab runs on Rock-Paper-Scissors, 20 seeded runs each: see how close each gets to the Nash equilibrium.

      Rock-Paper-Scissors · Fig. 3.2(a)Our simulation

      How this race was run

      • Task. Rock-Paper-Scissors (Fig. 3.2(a)): two agents play it again and again. Its only Nash equilibrium plays each action with probability 1/3.
      • Runs. 20,000 steps per run and 20 seeds (11–30) for every method the Interactive Lab runs on this game, measured every 500 steps.
      • Performance. Exploitability: how much the two agents together could gain by switching to best responses; it is 0 exactly at a Nash equilibrium (§4.4). Fictitious play and regret matching are scored on their empirical action frequencies, as the book plots them (Figures 6.5 and 6.14); the others on their current policies.
      • Settings. The Lab’s: IQL with Boltzmann exploration and the α chosen above; IGA-style gradient ascent with a fixed step; WoLF-PHC with α = 0.1 and a decaying δ; Nash-Q and CE-Q with ϵ = 0.2, decaying; one PSRO step is one PSRO iteration (a new best response).
      • Precomputed. The runs were computed in advance with the Lab’s own learners, so this page stays fast; the Lab trains the same learners live.

      Decision guide

      Which method should I use?

      Questions about your problem, one at a time. Independent learners are strong baselines, so compare against them. Not in the book

      Check yourself

      Tell them apart

      Each answer is in a column of the master table or the method’s section of the book.

      1Which of these is trained centrally and executed decentrally (CTDE)?

      VDN trains the sum of utilities on the common reward, yet each agent acts greedily on its own utility (§9.5). IQL is decentralized throughout; central Q-learning also acts centrally.

      2Which method models each other agent by counting its past actions?

      §6.3.1: in fictitious play each agent models each other agent’s policy as the empirical distribution of its past actions and best-responds to it.

      3Which method applies only to two-agent zero-sum stochastic games?

      §6.2.1: minimax Q-learning solves each stage game with a minimax solution, which is defined for two-agent zero-sum games.

      Notation

      Every symbol the site uses, in the book’s Summary of Notation order, with how to read it aloud and where it first appears.

      1. Read the two rulesTime is a superscript (sᵗ); the agent is a subscript (aᵢ).
      2. Take a symbol apartHover a part of an equation below to light its row.
      3. Look one upFilter by kind or search by name, such as alpha or γ.

      How to read the notation

      Three rules cover most symbols; the color key holds on every page.

      Time is a superscript

      st, at, rt, ht

      Read sᵗ as “s at time t”, not “s to the power t”.

      The agent is a subscript

      ai, ri, πi, a−i

      aᵢ is agent i’s action; −i means all agents except i.

      No subscript means joint

      a = (a1, …, an)

      a, o, r and π without an index are tuples over all agents.

      • Agent 1 (row player)
      • Agent 2 (column player)
      • Equilibrium or optimum
      • Pareto-optimal
